Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28 16:00 UTC
Duration: 1:02
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Atlas Head of ML), Sara Kim (Atlas Platform Eng), Jonah Blake (Atlas Infra Lead)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Redwood ran a workshop to align on benchmark methodology for runtime performance and apples-to-apples comparisons. Agreed action items: Redwood to supply prompt sets, load generator configs, benchmark template; Atlas to provide sequence length distribution, SLOs, and test infra details. Follow-up benchmark scheduled.

Topics:
- Benchmark goals and success criteria
- Prompt selection and distribution (short/med/long)
- Load generation: ramp, concurrency, qps, tail latency
- KV cache warm/cold behavior and measurement
- Batching strategies and latency percentiles
- Quantization tradeoffs and quality checks
- On-prem/VPC network constraints and reproducibility

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Marco Ruiz: yes can hear you, thanks Alex.
[00:05] Priya Singh: hi all, Priya from Redwood, SE on the call, i'll cover the bench methodology stuff.
[00:10] Sara Kim: hey, Sara here. we're mostly focused on production numbers — p95 and p99 and cost per 1k tokens.
[00:14] Jonah Blake: Jonah, infra. we'll be running this in our staging VPC initially. question about network egress.

[00:18] Alex Chen: great, quick agenda: one, align on goals and metrics; two, go through prompt sets and load-gen config; three, deep-dive on KV cache and batching measurables; four, quantization and apples-to-apples; five, next steps.

[00:32] Priya Singh: starting with goals — we usually recommend focusing on 3 metrics: throughput (RPS / tokens per second), latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), and cost per token. also success criteria like sustained p95 < X ms for your tail sensitive flows, and regressions no more than Y% vs baseline.
[00:48] Marco Ruiz: for Atlas our target is p95 < 200ms for short prompts (<=64 tokens) and p95 < 800ms for longer conversational flows (~512 tokens). cost target is less hard but want to quantify.

[00:58] Priya Singh: perfect, we'll parameterize prompt sets by sequence length distribution to match that. important note: when measuring p99 you must control for cold kv cache behavior — results vary a lot if the KV cache is cold vs warm.

[01:12] Sara Kim: can you explain how you define 'KV cache warm' in your benchmarks?

[01:15] Priya Singh: yes. warm means the model's KV cache has been populated via prefix tokens for that conversation or session — basically subsequent tokens after the same chat history reuse the cached keys/values. in our harness we run a warmup phase per session ID so that you see steady-state latencies. cold run is a single shot with no cache warmup. we capture both. note: sometimes transcription says K V cash or K V cache — people call it KV cash.

[01:33] Jonah Blake: from infra side we care about memory pressure on GPUs when KV cache scales across many sessions. do you simulate realistic session counts?

[01:40] Priya Singh: yes, in the load generator we model sessions and sticky routing. you can configure number of concurrent sessions and tokens per session; caching memory usage scales roughly linearly with concurrent active sessions and context length. we'll include a memory trace log during runs.

[01:55] Alex Chen: let's step through the prompt sets. we propose three buckets: short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-256), long (257-1024). For each bucket we provide ~50 distinct prompts to cover instruction, chat, and few-shot completions. prompts will be annotated with expected tokenization length and typical output length.

[02:13] Marco Ruiz: 50 each seems okay. can you include domain-y finance prompts to test hallucination/regression under quantization?

[02:18] Priya Singh: absolutely, we'll add a finance sub-bucket to the medium/long sets and include our evaluation checks — simple fidelity checks (e.g., numeric extraction) to compare outputs across quantization settings.

[02:26] Sara Kim: load generation — do you recommend sustained RPS or spike tests? we have bursty workloads.

[02:30] Priya Singh: both. baseline steady-state for throughput and then spike tests for tail behaviour — e.g., 5x traffic for 30s, then return to baseline. also test gradual ramp to observe autoscaling behavior for Dedicated or on-prem autoscaler. we provide JMeter and k6 configs, and a lightweight custom Go load-gen for token-level control.

[02:48] Jonah Blake: if we run on our staging VPC there will be network variability; how do we isolate network noise vs runtime latency?

[02:52] Priya Singh: good call. recommended approach: run the benchmark agent inside the same VPC (co-located) so you measure only the model runtime + intra-cluster network. for cross-region tests we explicitly measure network RT and separate it out in the spreadsheet. we'll also run synthetic loopback tests that measure pure inference time without HTTP overhead.

[03:10] Marco Ruiz: about apples-to-apples — we want to compare your hosted variant vs our on-prem model instance. how do you ensure parity in model version/quantization and kernel set?

[03:18] Alex Chen: key is to pin model file (same checkpoint), pin tokenizer version, and use identical quantization profiles. we provide a config template that lists model architecture, tokenizer SHA, transformer config, and quantization flags. we also recommend matching batch size and sequence length ceilings. where possible we run the same runtime build or at least the same kernel set; in some on-prem cases customers have slightly different GPU drivers — we annotate that in the results.

[03:38] Priya Singh: also important: some runtimes use different attention kernel selections for long sequences — we log the kernel selection per run and include it in the artifact so you can see if differences are due to kernels. this is one reason we capture an artifacts tarball with perf counters + nvprof-like summaries.

[03:56] Sara Kim: quantization — how do you measure quality regressions? we need a simple metric not full evals.

[04:01] Priya Singh: for benching we recommend a lightweight eval: a set of 200 gold prompts with deterministic extraction tasks (e.g., return a numeric answer, or structured JSON). we compute exact-match or token-level overlap and report delta vs FP16 baseline. for generation quality we also use log-perplexity and a small human-labeled set for subjective checks. if delta in exact-match > 2% we flag it.

[04:25] Marco Ruiz: ok that's helpful. also, for cost calculations we need to agree on token accounting — include request+response tokens, and account for KV cache hits if you precompute prefixes?

[04:34] Priya Singh: yes token accounting includes input tokens + output tokens. we explicitly annotate when prefix caching is used; if you precompute and store embeddings/prefixes, we separate that cost in an additional column.

[04:42] Jonah Blake: on batching: some runtimes batch across concurrent requests which increases throughput but can raise p95. how do you configure batching in tests?

[04:47] Priya Singh: we test three modes: no batching (strict single-request latency), dynamic batching (runtime decides within a max latency window), and fixed micro-batches (e.g., batch sizes 2/4/8). we sweep the batch timeout parameter and report p50/p95/p99 and throughput. we also provide a plot of throughput vs p95 so you can pick acceptable tradeoffs.

[05:06] Alex Chen: note that dynamic batching behavior can depend on request size distribution and concurrency, so we run both synthetic uniform-size tests and a mixed-size distribution that matches your seq length histogram.

[05:18] Marco Ruiz: how do you handle retries and transient infra errors in the benchmark harness? we don't want retries skewing the latency numbers.

[05:23] Priya Singh: harness treats retries separately: we log them as errors and exclude retried requests from latency percentiles but capture an error rate KPI. for p99 we recommend excluding requests that had to be retried because of infra flakiness but include them in availability metrics.

[05:36] Sara Kim: for on-prem runs we need to supply IAM, KMS, and image installation instructions. can you share the Private deployment checklist?

[05:43] Alex Chen: yes we'll send the Private deployment checklist and the on-prem install guide. it includes KMS integration notes, SAML/SSO setup, and network ports. we'll note the minimum kernel/driver versions we validated.

[05:53] Priya Singh: small note on measurements: when measuring memory and KV cache footprint we run with multiple concurrent session profiles and collect GPU memory snapshots every 10s; we include a CSV time series so you can see memory pressure during spike tests.

[06:05] Marco Ruiz: sounds good. can you also surface worst-case cpu/gpu utilization during long sequences? we had runaway kernels in a prior test.

[06:11] Priya Singh: yes we capture GPU utilization, SM occupancy, host CPU, and process-level memory. we'll include flamegraphs if requested, but for the initial pass a utilization time series should suffice.

[06:21] Jonah Blake: any gotchas with quantization and KV cache interaction? i've seen cases where int8 quantized kernels behave strangely with long context.

[06:28] Priya Singh: good call — some quantized kernels trade off numerical stability for perf. we run a stability check across long sequences (1k tokens) to watch for divergence in logits. if divergence grows beyond a threshold we mark the profile as unstable. also we recommend A/B testing quantization profiles per workload.

[06:43] Marco Ruiz: for apples-to-apples comparing your hosted results to our on-prem, how do we attribute differences to HW vs config?

[06:48] Alex Chen: we annotate hardware spec (GPU model, driver, CPU, interconnect), kernel versions, and runtime flags. then we run a small calibration micro-benchmark (single-layer matmul + attention kernel) to get a baseline flop/s and memory bandwidth estimate — that helps attribute delta to hardware.

[07:05] Priya Singh: we'll also provide a 'calibration run' script you can run locally — it's a tiny workload that exercises attention and KV cache so you can compare perf counters.

[07:13] Sara Kim: ok practical next steps: we want the prompt sets and the load-gen configs so we can review and run in our staging.

[07:19] Alex Chen: action items: Priya will send prompt sets and JMeter/k6 configs; Alex will send apples-to-apples spreadsheet + Private deployment checklist; Marco will give us sequence length distribution and SLOs. we've captured these.

[07:29] Marco Ruiz: timeline — we'd like to run our first canary benchmarks week of 2/10. is that workable?

[07:33] Alex Chen: yes, that fits. we'll work with your infra calendar. we'll also set up a short workshop to walk your team through running the harness.

[07:41] Priya Singh: one more note: for reporting we output a standardized artifact: CSV of raw latencies, a summary JSON with metrics, and an HTML dashboard with plots. we'll attach kernel selection logs and the artifact tarball.

[07:53] Jonah Blake: will you include the runtime version and a reproducible Dockerfile for the harness?

[07:58] Priya Singh: yes, we'll include Dockerfile and SHA hashes for all binaries and the exact runtime commit we used.

[08:05] Sara Kim: any concerns about sharing these artifacts with our security team?

[08:08] Alex Chen: for sensitive artifacts we can share over your secure S3 or use our Private transfer method; we'll redact customer-identifying info in public artifacts. we'll also send SOC2/ISO docs with the checklist.

[08:18] Marco Ruiz: ok thanks, that gives us confidence.

[08:21] Alex Chen: wrap-up: recap and next steps — Priya send prompts and load-gen; Alex send benchmark template and security docs; Marco provide seq distribution and SLOs; schedule follow-up week of 2/10 for canary run.

[08:36] Priya Singh: any final q's?
[08:38] Marco Ruiz: none from me, thanks.
[08:40] Sara Kim: none. thanks all.
[08:42] Jonah Blake: thanks everyone.
[08:44] Alex Chen: great, we'll follow up via email with artifacts. thanks all, bye.
